comparator.name: Information Science (Informatiekunde)
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 programme-specific OER annex defines a 180-EC Informatiekunde bachelor comprising a 135-EC major and 45-EC profiling space. The major contains 75 EC of compulsory courses, one complete 30-EC study path, 15 EC of additional major electives and the compulsory 15-EC Onderzoeksproject. For the generic target, Informatiesystemen is selected because it most directly continues the programme’s broad organisational and information-systems identity; this choice is independent of UCR fit. Cognitie en emotie and Usability engineering en user experience are selected as the first two officially listed eligible courses outside that path. Zero-credit tutorial activities are excluded from the 180 EC.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic Informatiekunde bachelor and does not name one of the three compulsory study paths. Informatiesystemen most directly continues the mandatory organisational, process and information-system core and the programme’s stated role as a bridge between ICT and organisations. It is therefore selected as the broadest expression of the target’s academic identity, independently of UCR fit.

alternatives.label: Information systems, organisations & digital society
alternatives.concept: Combines programming, databases, data science and computational methods with user-centred design, organisational change, research methods and responsible digital governance. It follows Utrecht’s broad people-organisation-technology orientation while acknowledging that UCR lacks its dedicated process-modelling, digital-ecosystem, product-software, security and compulsory research sequence.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum gives comparable weight to computational information systems, organisations, users and the societal implications of digital technology.
progression: All formal prerequisites occur in earlier semesters and every course is assigned to a planned 2026–29 offering. Research and organisational foundations precede advanced methods, algorithms, AI and digital-transformation work; six 300-level courses are included.

alternatives.label: Data science & computational information
alternatives.concept: Retains programming, databases, organisational context and responsible technology while shifting 30 EC toward linear algebra, numerical and systems modelling, probability and advanced machine learning. This route develops the programme’s explicit data-and-decision interest rather than treating information science as software development alone.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed schedule adds four mathematics and data courses and removes four design, qualitative and organisational courses, making data modelling the dominant differentiating strand.
alternatives.distinctness: Linear Algebra, Computational & Numerical Methods, Linear Systems and Probability & Statistics replace Consumer Product Design, Qualitative Research Methodology, Psychology of Organizations & Leadership and Persuasive Communication. Each curriculum therefore contains 30 EC absent from the other.
progression: All formal prerequisites occur in earlier semesters and every course is assigned to a planned 2026–29 offering. Mathematical Methods precedes linear algebra, numerical methods and probability; programming precedes advanced algorithms and AI optimisation; six 300-level courses are included.

alternatives.label: Human-centred & socio-technical systems
alternatives.concept: Retains programming, databases, data science and organisational analysis but shifts the advanced programme toward perception, social psychology, interaction, language, institutional trust and technology adoption. It develops the explicit human-needs and social-impact interests as one coherent study of how people and institutions use and respond to digital systems.
alternatives.labelReason: The final curriculum combines a technical information-system foundation with a sustained psychology, cognition, sociology, user-design and organisational sequence.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest programme, Introduction to Brain & Behavior, Social Psychology, Modern Sociology, Perception & Action, Higher Order Functions, New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory and Psycholinguistics replace Mathematical Methods, Logic & Discrete Mathematics, Qualitative Research Methodology, Ethics, Algorithms & Data Structures, Optimization Methods in AI and Neural Networks & Deep Learning. The 52.5-EC shift creates a human-centred socio-technical curriculum and also exceeds the pairwise 30-EC floor against the data-science alternative.
progression: All formal prerequisites occur in earlier semesters and every course is assigned to a planned 2026–29 offering. Introduction to Brain & Behavior precedes the cognitive-science courses; Introduction to Sociology and Modern Sociology precede the advanced social-theory course as an advisory progression; six 300-level courses are included.

selection.assessment: The closest broad Information Science response is feasible. The direct interest in using data to improve decisions supports a coherent data-science curriculum, while the direct interests in designing around human needs and analysing social impact support a coherent human-centred socio-technical curriculum. The remaining direct organisational and information-exchange interests are substantively represented in the closest programme. All three included programmes pass the qualitative and pairwise 30-EC distinctness tests, so production stops at the permitted maximum of three.

blocks: Introduction to Programming directly addresses the Python programming and computational-thinking component, with different scope and credits.
Database Management Systems directly addresses database and data modelling, with different scope and credits.
UCR has no selected course that reproduces the combined human, computer-mediated and visual information-exchange component.
UCR has no selected dedicated process-modelling course.
UCR has no selected course that reproduces the programme’s systematic information-system development methods.
UCR has no selected course that reproduces digital-ecosystem architecture.
UCR has no selected course dedicated to product-software architecture, markets and licensing.
UCR has no selected dedicated information-security course.
Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations addresses organisational and management foundations, while the comparator applies them specifically to ICT.
Strategy & Digital Transformation directly addresses strategic organisational change through ICT, with different scope and credits.
Consumer Product Design contributes user-needs analysis and iterative design, while focusing on products more broadly than interactive systems.
Introduction to Brain & Behavior supplies foundations in cognition and emotion relevant to technology use, with broader behavioural-science scope.
Perception & Action supplies human perceptual and motor foundations for usability, but does not reproduce the comparator’s full UX-engineering methodology.
UCR sociology, computing and ethics courses address parts of people, society and ICT, but no one selected course reproduces the integrated compulsory component.
Research Methods & Statistics directly supports scientific research design and analysis, with broader cross-disciplinary scope.
The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops analysis, argument and communication, though it is not Information-Science-specific academic-skills training.
UCR’s optional independent-research opportunity is shown separately against the compulsory 15-EC Onderzoeksproject; it is not part of the fixed 180-EC UCR programme.
The genuine 45-EC profiling space is preserved without inventing a specific Utrecht minor, exchange or elective package.

notes.text: Utrecht University integrates organisations, information systems, human-computer interaction and data through a compulsory core, a complete study path, a 15-EC research project and dedicated process, ecosystem, product-software and security components. UCR can combine substantial programming, databases, data analysis, user research, organisational change, cognition and responsible-technology study, but distributes them across computing, business, psychology, sociology, communication and philosophy rather than reproducing that structured Information Science sequence.
